newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-UNITED MACHINE COMES OFF THE RAILS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-UNITED MACHINE COMES OFF THE RAILS.

text.p: Manchester United's all-conquering machine has suddenly jumped off the rails with a fourth humbling defeat in a fortnight and fans and foes alike are sifting through the wreckage to work out why.

The loss of form of the club's "French genius" Eric Cantona, the departure of defensive colossus Steve Bruce and the absence of wing wizard Ryan Giggs through injury are the most plausible explanations put forward for the stunning turn in fortune.
United's manager Alex Ferguson will on Wednesday be celebrating 10 years at Old Trafford, during which time he has revived the glories they knew in the 1950s and 60s under Sir Matt Busby.
But instead of reflecting on winning the championship three times in four years, including twice adding the F.A. Cup for an unprecedented "double double", Fergie has troubles on his mind.
United are undoubtedly handicapped by the loss of form of enigmatic French star Eric Cantona, referred to with respect and affection as "mon genius" by Ferguson.

Cantona's sudden inability to exert any influnce on United's play has not been helped by Ferguson's decision to play him at times as a lone striker rather than in the deeper attacking role he relishes.

But their problems may be traced more accurately to the absence of 35-year-old defender Bruce, who was allowed to leave in the summer so that he could play out his time down in the first division with Birmingham City.

Bruce was United's captain, often their only non-international on the pitch, and Ferguson has admitted: "There will be occasions when we suffer from the loss of a defensive collosus such as Bruce. His sheer enthusiasm and priceless will to win cannot easily be replaced."
Bruce was a leader who followed another natural captain, Bryan Robson, giving United continuity when they began to dominate the English game.

Bruce's loss of pace as he played on at the highest level into his mid-30s was sometimes exposed at the heart of United's defence. Now he is missed for his commitment, his motivation, his organisation and his advice to young players around him.
Bruce's value became clear when United began their bad spell by losing 5-0 to Newcastle. Then unrated Southampton scored six against them the following week.

This was followed by their first home defeat in 40 years of European competition -- 1-0 by unrated Turkish side Fenerbahce in the European Cup -- a performance which disproved the theory that United were saving their best for Europe.

Next came another loss in the premier league when Chelsea beat them 2-1 at Old Trafford on Saturday, their first home defeat in the league in almost two years. A month ago, a fourth such humiliation would have seemed as unlikely as four successive days of sunshine on murky Manchester.
Unflappable Danish goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel, as off-form as the rest of the team, was blamed for not coming out to stop Chelsea's second goal from Gianluca Vialli.
"Originally I thought that I could not get the ball but when it was too late I knew that I could have got it because he stopped as well," he said.
"When you are in a spell like this you take the wrong decision every time. It will just be a case of getting one bit of luck, one break and we will be back."

Cantona as a captain is subdued. One former England skipper pointed out: "When the team is playing well, he gives you the extra that wins championships. But he is different when the rest of the team is struggling."

Injuries have hit United badly. They are without England defender Gary Pallister, a player who would also be an obvious candidate if Ferguson were to risk upsetting Cantona by trying an alternative captain.

Missing, too, are Phil Neville, still only 19 and a defender of true potential alongside his elder brother Gary, as well as the attacking threat of Giggs, whose pace from the wings interacts with Cantona and gives United another option.

Ferguson has further flavoured United's international menu this season by introducing Karel Poborsky, Jordi Cryuff and Ole Gunnar Solskjar, all capable of tickling the taste buds but yet to produce a banquet for the United faithful to feast on.
Ferguson, who will be 55 next month, has won three championships, three F.A. Cups, the League Cup and the European Cup Winners' Cup for United.
Success has cost a comparatively modest six million pounds ($9.6 dollars) when his buying is balanced against his selling.
His target remains the European Cup and United should still qualify for the knock-out stage despite the Fenerbahce embarrassment.

When he has everyone fit and the newcomers fitted-in, he will have options which will be the envy of every other premier league manager. He will then have to demand that his men rediscover their obsession with winning.
